Exact Covariance Structure and Efficient Computation for L-Comments

**Abstract**

L-moments are useful summary statistics and so have been widely employed in statistical analysis. L-comoments provide a multivariate generalization of L-moments. Joint finite- sample covariance structure, which represents the sampling uncertainty, of L-comoments is less well understood than that of univariate L-moments. We thus derive exact finite-sample covariance formulas for sample L-comoments using explicit conditional U-statistic kernels. We further construct an asymptotic projection estimator and an unbiased estimator of the finite-sample covariance matrix and develop positive-definite corrections. An efficient rank-prefix algorithm evaluates the full unbiased covariance estimator in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time without enumerating disjoint subsets. Numerical experiments demonstrate substantial computational savings. The results provide a basis for first-order covariance approximations for L-comoment ratios and for subsequent multivariate L-moment estimation.

**Keywords:** Concomitant; U-statistic; covariance estimation; Gini covariance; exact unbiased estimation; L-moments; rank-prefix algorithm.

**MSC 2020:** 62G05, 62H20, 62G30.

## 1 Introduction

L-moments summarize distributional location, scale, and shape through linear combinations of order statistics and require only first moments for their existence (Hosking, 1990). Methods based on L-moments have been widely used for distributional analysis and parameter estimation, notably through the method of L-moments estimation. Compared with conventional moments,<tbc>

<tbc>L-moments are generally less sensitive to outlying observations and sampling variability. In some distributional settings, L-moment estimators are computationally efficient and can also be competitive with likelihood-based estimators, particularly for small samples (for example, Hosking, 1990; Sankarasubramanian and Srinivasan, 1999; Hosking and Wallis, 1997; Murshed et al., 2014; Shin et al., 2025). These properties make an understanding of their sampling distributions and finite-sample uncertainty especially valuable.

For univariate L-moments, Elamir and Seheult (2004) derived exact finite-sample variance- covariance formulas and distribution-free unbiased estimators, including a weighted order- statistic implementation. They also considered approximate standard errors for ratios of sample L-moments. Their findings provide a useful basis for studying the finite-sample behavior of L- moment statistics, which cannot in general be fully characterized by asymptotic approximations alone.

As a multivariate generalization, Serfling and Xiao (2007) introduced directional L-comoments and L-comoment matrices, developed concomitant and U-statistic representations, and investigated asymptotic properties. They also noted that general U-statistic theory provides a route to exact variances and unbiased covariance estimation. However, explicit joint finite-sample covariance formulas for second and third L-comoments, together with an efficient unbiased covariance estimator, were not developed there. To the best of our knowledge, a comparable explicit treatment has not subsequently been available. Motivated by the univariate work of Elamir and Seheult (2004), we address this gap. The general U-statistic overlap principle that we use is standard; our contribution is its explicit application to L-comoments.

L-comoments and related multivariate L-moment methods have been used in regional flood analysis (Chebana and Ouarda, 2007; Akinsoji et al., 2026), drought regionalization (Zhang et al., 2012), bivariate drought modeling (Abdi et al., 2017), and rainfall-frequency homogeneity studies (Shin et al., 2018). Related multivariate methods arise in homogeneity testing under spatial dependence (Šimková, 2017), joint marine extremes (Bai et al., 2023), and process monitoring (Arslan et al., 2025). In these applications, the sample L-comoment matrix is used to summarize the dependence between the measured variables. In regional frequency analysis, for example, sample L-comoments and their ratios are compared across sites with short records, and their sampling variability is typically assessed by simulation from fitted parametric models (Chebana and Ouarda, 2007; Šimková, 2017). Our object of study is different: it is the _sampling covariance matrix_ of these estimated L-comoments, which quantifies their uncertainty. Throughout the paper, "L-comoment" refers to the population quantity or its sample estimate, whereas "sampling covariance matrix" refers only to the covariance of the estimators.

Relative to Serfling and Xiao (2007) and Elamir and Seheult (2004), the main new contributions of this study are threefold.

_First,_ whereas Serfling and Xiao (2007) obtained only the asymptotic covariance of the sample L-comoments, we give closed-form conditional kernels _M_<sub>2,1</sub>, _M_<sub>3,1</sub>, and _M_<sub>3,2</sub> for L-comoments,<tbc>

together with a canonical Hoeffding decomposition, so that every entry of the exact \(4\times 4\) and \(6\times 6\) covariance matrices is expressed through explicit expectations rather than through the general overlap identity alone. As a special case, this gives the exact joint covariance of the two directional Gini covariance estimators (Remark 3.3).

_Second,_ when _X_ and _Y_ are independent, we obtain a fully explicit covariance matrix.

_Third,_ we show that the exactly unbiased covariance estimator can be computed in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time, much faster than its direct evaluation, which requires _O(n_<sup>6</sup>) operations. The fast algorithm combines an overlap inclusion-exclusion identity with rank-prefix sums.

We also study a consistent positive-semidefinite (PSD) estimator of the leading asymptotic covariance; it also covers fourth-order L-comoments and is computed in _O(n_log_n_) time. In addition, we establish the first-order consistency of the unbiased estimator and give its positive-definite (PD) regularization. Numerical experiments confirm that the fast and direct algorithms agree and compare their computing times. The experiments also show that individual unbiased covariance estimates need not be PSD. These results are practically relevant because L-comoment-based regional and bivariate frequency analyses often rely on short records, for example a few decades of annual data (Hosking and Wallis, 1997; Chebana and Ouarda, 2007). For such sample sizes, asymptotic standard errors can be noticeably biased. Section 6 quantifies this bias and the accompanying bias-variance trade-off between unbiased and asymptotic covariance estimators.

The exact covariances of the L-comoments can also be used to approximate the covariances of L-comoment ratios by a first-order Taylor expansion, as in the delta method (Oehlert, 1992; van der Vaart, 1998); these approximations are given in Appendix E. Parameter estimation using L-comoments is not developed here. Related work uses L-moment methods for copula parameter estimation (Brahimi et al., 2015), but copula modeling and parameter estimation are beyond the scope of the present study. Sample L-comoments can already be computed using functions such as `Lcomoment.Lk12` and `Lcomoment.matrix` in the R package `lmomco` (Asquith, 2026).

Section 2 introduces L-comoments and their sample representations. Section 3 derives the exact covariance structure. Section 4 develops covariance estimation, and Section 5 gives the efficient computation of the covariance estimators and their PSD and PD corrections. Section 6 reports numerical experiments, Section 7 discusses implications and extensions, and Section 8 concludes. The appendices collect background facts, derivations, computational details, and the covariance of L-comoment ratios.

## 2 Directional L-comoments and sample constructions ### 2.1 Definitions Let _Zb_=(_Xb,Yb_), _b_=1_,...,n_, be independent and identically distributed (iid) pairs from a continuous bivariate distribution. The two coordinates of each pair may be dependent. We refer to _X_ and _Y_ as the marginal variables, or simply the margins, and to _FX_ and _FY_ as their marginal distribution functions. We write \(\mu_X=\mathbb{E}(X)\) and \(\mu_Y=\mathbb{E}(Y)\), and _Z_=(_X,Y_) denotes a generic pair with the same distribution as _Zb_. Assume \(\mathbb{E}(X^2+Y^2)<\infty\) whenever covariance is considered. For _m_=2,3,4, the _m_th L-moment of _X_ (Hosking, 1990) can be written as \(\lambda_m(X)=\mathbb{E}(XP_{m-1}\{F_X(X)\}),\) (2.1) where _P__m_-1 is the shifted Legendre polynomial of degree _m_-1 on \[0,1\], given by \(P_1(u)=2u-1,P_2(u)=6u^2-6u+1,P_3(u)=20u^3-30u^2+12u-1.\) (2.2) Here \(\lambda_2(X)\) is the L-scale of _X_, \(\lambda_3(X)\) measures the skewness of _X_, and \(\lambda_4(X)\) measures the kurtosis of _X_. The ratios \(\lambda_3(X)/\lambda_2(X)\) and \(\lambda_4(X)/\lambda_2(X)\) are the L-skewness and the L-kurtosis of _X_ (Hosking, 1990). Replacing _FX(X_) by _FY(Y_) in (2.1) defines the L-comoments of Serfling and Xiao (2007), a bivariate extension of L-moments. **Definition 2.1** (Directional L-comoments)**.** For _m_=2,3,4, the _m_th directional L-comoment of _X_ with respect to _Y_ and that of _Y_ with respect to _X_ are \(\lambda_m^{[XY]}=\mathbb{E}(XP_{m-1}\{F_Y(Y)\}),\lambda_m^{[YX]}=\mathbb{E}(YP_{m-1}\{F_X(X)\}).\) (2.3) In the \[_XY_\] direction, that is, \(\lambda_2^{[XY]}=\mathbb{E}[X\{2F_Y(Y)-1\}],\)
\(\lambda_3^{[XY]}=\mathbb{E}[X\{6F_Y(Y)^2-6F_Y(Y)+1\}],\)
\(\lambda_4^{[XY]}=\mathbb{E}[X\{20F_Y(Y)^3-30F_Y(Y)^2+12F_Y(Y)-1\}],\) and the \[_YX_\] direction is obtained by exchanging _X_ and _Y_ . The two directional L-comoments \(\lambda_m^{[XY]}\) and \(\lambda_m^{[YX]}\) are not equal in general, which is why we call them "directional" (asymmetric in the terminology of Serfling and Xiao (2007)). Since only directional L-comoments are considered in this paper, we simply call them L-comoments from now on; the direction is indicated by the superscript \[_XY_\] or \[_YX_\].

## 2.2 Representation and interpretation of L-comoments

L-comoments can also be written in terms of concomitants of order statistics, in the same way as univariate L-moments are written in terms of order statistics (Hosking, 1990). Consider a conceptual sample (_X_<sub>1</sub>_,Y_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,(X<sub>k</sub>,Y<sub>k</sub>_) of size _k_ from the distribution of (_X,Y_). If we order the sample by the _Y_ values and obtain the order statistics \(Y_{1:k}<\cdots<Y_{k:k}\), then the _X_ value paired with _Y<sub>r:k</sub>_ is called the _concomitant_ of _Y<sub>r:k</sub>_ and is denoted by _X_<sub>\[_r:k_\]</sub> (Yang, 1977; David and Nagaraja, 2003; Jamalizadeh and Balakrishnan, 2012). Note that _X_<sub>\[_r:k_\]</sub> is not the _r_th order statistic _X<sub>r:k</sub>_ of the _X_ values. It is the _X_ value of the pair whose _Y_ value has rank _r_, so _X_<sub>\[1:_k_\]</sub>_,...,X_<sub>\[_k:k_\]</sub> are in general not in increasing order. By Proposition 6 of Serfling and Xiao (2007),

\(\lambda_2^{[XY]}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\big(X_{[2:2]}-X_{[1:2]}\big),\lambda_3^{[XY]}=\frac{1}{3}\mathbb{E}\big(X_{[3:3]}-2X_{[2:3]}+X_{[1:3]}\big),\lambda_4^{[XY]}=\frac{1}{4}\mathbb{E}\big(X_{[4:4]}-3X_{[3:4]}+3X_{[2:4]}-X_{[1:4]}\big).\text{(2.4)}\)

In Appendix B.1, (2.4) is derived from Definition 2.1. Thus, if two pairs are drawn and the pair with the larger _Y_ value is identified, \(\lambda_2^{[XY]}\) is half the expected difference between the _X_ value of that pair and the _X_ value of the other pair. Similarly, if three pairs are drawn and sorted by their _Y_ values, \(\lambda_3^{[XY]}\) compares the _X_ value of the middle pair with the _X_ values of the two outer pairs.

Serfling and Xiao (2007) called \(\lambda_2^{[XY]}\), \(\lambda_3^{[XY]}\), and \(\lambda_4^{[XY]}\) the L-covariance, the L-coskewness, and the L-cokurtosis. They called the standardized versions \(\tau_m^{[XY]}=\lambda_m^{[XY]}/\lambda_2(X)\) and \(\tau_m^{[YX]}=\lambda_m^{[YX]}/\lambda_2(Y)\) the L-comoment coefficients, and \(\tau_2^{[XY]}\) in particular the L-correlation. The L- correlation lies in \[-1,1\], and it equals \(\pm 1\) if and only if _X_ is a strictly monotone function of _Y_ (Serfling and Xiao, 2007, Proposition 4). Under linear regression of _X_ on _Y_ with affinely equivalent margins (that is, _Y_ has the same distribution as \(\alpha+\beta X\) for some \(\alpha\) and some \(\beta>0\)), as in the bivariate normal distribution, it equals the Pearson correlation (Serfling and Xiao, 2007, Proposition 3), but it requires only finite first moments. Replacing _X_ by _F<sub>X</sub>(X_) in \(\tau_2^{[XY]}\) gives 12Cov{_F<sub>X</sub>(X),F<sub>Y</sub>(Y_)}, which is Spearman’s rank correlation. Each L-comoment carries the unit of its first variable, so it is divided by the L-scale of that variable. At order two, these coefficients are related to directional Gini correlations, and several symmetric Gini constructions have also been studied (Sang et al., 2016; Vanderford et al., 2020). In the rest of this paper we restrict attention to _m_=2,3, which are the orders most frequently used in applications. The fourth L-comoment is included above for completeness; Remark 4.7 and Section 7 discuss the extension of our results to order four and beyond.

L-comoments are rank-based analogues of conventional cross-moments. In particular, the second L-comoment is<tbc>

\(\lambda_2^{[XY]}=2Cov\{X,F_Y(Y)\},\)

<tbc>which is twice the Gini covariance of _X_ with respect to _Y_ (Schechtman and Yitzhaki, 1987;<tbc>

<tbc>Yitzhaki and Schechtman, 2013; Carcea and Serfling, 2015). The third L-comoment is<tbc>

\(\lambda_3^{[XY]}=6\mathrm{Cov}\{X,W\},W=\{F_Y(Y)-1/2\}^2.\)

<tbc>It is a rank-based analogue of the coskewness \(\mathbb{E}\{(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)^2\}\) (Rubinstein, 1973; Harvey and Siddique, 2000), obtained by replacing \(Y-\mu_Y\) with _F<sub>Y</sub>(Y_)-1/2 (Serfling and Xiao, 2007, Section 3.1.4). Since _F<sub>Y</sub>(Y_) is uniform on (0,1), E(_W_)=1/12, and therefore

\(\lambda_3^{[XY]}=6\{\mathbb{E}(XW)-\mathbb{E}(X)\mathbb{E}(W)\}=6\mathbb{E}\{X(W-1/12)\}.\)

The weight _W_-1/12 is positive when _F<sub>Y</sub>(Y)\<_0.21 or _F<sub>Y</sub>(Y)\>_0.79, that is, when _Y_ lies in one of its two tails. The weight is negative when _Y_ lies in the central part of its distribution. Hence \(\lambda_3^{[XY]}>0\) when _X_ is on average larger for values of _Y_ in its tails than for values of _Y_ near its median, and \(\lambda_3^{[XY]}<0\) in the opposite case. For example, \(\lambda_3^{[XY]}=0\) for the bivariate normal distribution, because E(_X|Y_) is linear in _Y_ and _W_ is symmetric about the median of _Y_ . This is why \(\lambda_3^{[XY]}\) plays the role of a coskewness: like \(\mathbb{E}\{(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)^2\}\), it is positive when large values of _X_ occur with extreme values of _Y_ in either direction. Unlike the univariate L-skewness, the L-coskewness \(\lambda_3^{[XY]}\) is not unit-free: it has the units of _X_ and is invariant to monotone transformations of _Y_ . However, the ratio \(\tau_3^{[XY]}=\lambda_3^{[XY]}/\lambda_2(X)\) is unit-free, because its numerator and its denominator both have the units of _X_.

When _Y=X_, the L-comoments reduce to the univariate L-moments. The Gini covariance has been studied extensively as a single measure (Yitzhaki and Schechtman, 2013). In applications, however, L-comoments of several orders are used jointly, for example in multivariate regional frequency analysis (Chebana and Ouarda, 2007; Akinsoji et al., 2026) and copula estimation (Brahimi et al., 2015). Such joint use requires the joint sampling covariance of the estimated L-comoments, which is the subject of this paper.

## 2.3 Estimation of L-comoments

To estimate \(\lambda_m^{[XY]}\) from a sample, we follow the approach of Hosking (1990) for univariate L-moments. Each univariate L-moment is the expectation of a simple function of a conceptual sample of size _m_. For example, \(\lambda_2(X)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}(X_{2:2}-X_{1:2})\). For two observations _x<sub>i</sub>_ and _x<sub>j</sub>_, the corresponding function is \(\frac{1}{2}(x_{2:2}-x_{1:2})=\frac{1}{2}|x_i-x_j|\). Averaging it over all pairs of observations gives the unbiased estimator

\(\widehat{\lambda}_2(X)=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}^{-1}\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{2}|x_i-x_j|.\)

Higher-order sample L-moments are obtained in the same way from subsamples of size _m_ (Hosking, 1990).

L-comoments are estimated by the same principle. The function that is averaged over subsamples is called a kernel. Write _z<sub>i</sub>_=(_x<sub>i</sub>,y<sub>i</sub>_) for an observed pair. A kernel of order _m_<tbc>

takes _m_ distinct pairs _z_<sub>1</sub>_,...,z<sub>m</sub>_ and sorts them by their _y_ values. Let _x_<sub>\[1\]</sub>_,...,x_<sub>\[_m_\]</sub> be the corresponding _x_ values, that is, the concomitants within these _m_ pairs. The kernel combines these concomitants with the coefficients inside the expectations in (2.4). The order-two symmetric kernel is therefore<tbc>

\(H_2^{[XY]}(z_1,z_2)=\frac{x_{[2]}-x_{[1]}}{2}=\frac{(x_1-x_2)\mathrm{sgn}(y_1-y_2)}{2},\) (2.5)

<tbc>where sgn(_t_) equals 1, 0, or -1 according as _t\>_0, _t_=0, or _t\<_0, and the order-three symmetric kernel is

\(H_3^{[XY]}(z_1,z_2,z_3)=\frac{x_{[1]}-2x_{[2]}+x_{[3]}}{3}.\) (2.6)

The kernels \(H_m^{[YX]}\) are obtained by exchanging the roles of the _x_ and _y_ coordinates. The kernel \(H_2^{[XY]}\) lies between two familiar kernels: replacing sgn(_y_<sub>1</sub>-_y_<sub>2</sub>) by _y_<sub>1</sub>-_y_<sub>2</sub> in (2.5) gives the kernel (_x_<sub>1</sub>-_x_<sub>2</sub>)(_y_<sub>1</sub>-_y_<sub>2</sub>)/2 of the sample covariance, and replacing _x_<sub>1</sub>-_x_<sub>2</sub> by sgn(_x_<sub>1</sub>-_x_<sub>2</sub>) gives the kernel sgn(_x_<sub>1</sub>-_x_<sub>2</sub>)sgn(_y_<sub>1</sub>-_y_<sub>2</sub>) of Kendall’s tau. All these kernels are symmetric, that is, invariant under permutations of their arguments, because the pairs are first sorted by one coordinate. Symmetric kernels of this kind are standard in U-statistic theory (Hoeffding, 1948; Serfling, 1980; Lee, 1990), which is the main tool of this paper; the facts used repeatedly are collected in Appendix A.

We now construct estimators of the L-comoments from the sample. Since the two directions are estimated from the same pairs, we treat them jointly in vector form. Write

\(\unknown_m=(\lambda_m^{[XY]},\lambda_m^{[YX]})^\mathsf{T},H_m=(H_m^{[XY]},H_m^{[YX]})^\mathsf{T}.\)

For an index set \(I=\{i_1,\dots,i_m\}\subset\{1,\dots,n\}\), write _Z<sub>I</sub>_=(_Z_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,Z<sub>i<sub>m</sub></sub>_), so that **_H_**_<sub>m</sub>(Z<sub>I</sub>_)=**_H_**_<sub>m</sub>(Z_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,Z<sub>i<sub>m</sub></sub>_); by symmetry, the order of the indices does not matter.

For _m_=2,3 and \(a\in\{[XY],[YX]\}\), the kernel \(H_m^a\) evaluated at any _m_ distinct pairs has mean \(\lambda_m^a\); that is,<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}\{H_m(Z_I)\}=\unknown_m.\)

<tbc>This follows from (2.4), and a proof is given in Appendix B.1. We therefore estimate \(\unknown_m\) by the complete U-statistic

\(\widehat{\unknown}_m=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{m}^{-1}\sum_{I\subset\{1,\dots,n\},|I|=m}H_m(Z_I),m=2,3,\) (2.7)

which averages the kernel over all \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{m}\) subsets of size _m_. This estimator is unbiased for \(\unknown_m\). Each kernel is a linear combination of _x_ values or of _y_ values, so it is square integrable when \(\mathbb{E}(X^2+Y^2)<\infty\). Serfling and Xiao (2007) also gave this U-statistic representation.

The sample means <o>_X_</o> and <o>_Y_</o> are U-statistics of order one with kernels \(H_1^{[XY]}(z)=x\) and \(H_1^{[YX]}(z)=y\); they are included in the covariance matrix of Section 4.

The estimator (2.7) also has a simple weighted-sum form. Let _X_<sub>\[_q:n_\]</sub> be the concomitant of the _q_th smallest _Y_ value in the sample; as in Section 2, _X_<sub>\[_q:n_\]</sub> is not the _q_th order statistic of the _X_ values. Then the complete U-statistic (2.7) can be written as a weighted sum of the concomitants (Serfling and Xiao, 2007, Section 3.3):

\(\widehat{\lambda}_m^{[XY]}=\sum_{q=1}^nw_{m,q}X_{[q:n]},w_{2,q}=\frac{2q-n-1}{n(n-1)},w_{3,q}=\frac{6q^2-6(n+1)q+(n+1)(n+2)}{n(n-1)(n-2)}.\) (2.8)

The weights follow by counting how often each pair occupies each position in the kernels; Appendix B gives the details. The weights _w_<sub>2_,q_</sub> require \(n\ge 2\), and the weights _w_<sub>3_,q_</sub> require \(n\ge 3\). They satisfy \(\sum_qw_{m,q}=0\). To make the estimating equations (2.7) and (2.8) more concrete, Appendix B.3 restates both in elementary terms, gives the equivalent probability- weighted-moment form of (2.8), and evaluates both for a sample of size five.

We collect the four L-comoments and their estimators as

\(\unknown=(\lambda_2^{[XY]},\lambda_2^{[YX]},\lambda_3^{[XY]},\lambda_3^{[YX]})^\unknown,\widehat{\unknown}=(\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[XY]},\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[YX]},\widehat{\lambda}_3^{[XY]},\widehat{\lambda}_3^{[YX]})^\unknown.\)

By (2.7), \(\widehat{\unknown}\) is unbiased for \(\unknown\). Serfling and Xiao (2007, Proposition 8) showed that, under second-moment assumptions, the sample L-comoments of one direction are asymptotically multivariate normal. Their asymptotic covariance matrix is the corresponding block of _B_<sub>1</sub>_/n_ in Theorem 4.1 below. This approximation can be poor for the sample sizes at which L- comoments are typically used. In hydrology, for example, at-site records often contain only 20 to 50 observations, and Section 6.3 shows that the asymptotic covariance then understates the finite-sample covariance. Moreover, applications such as discordancy and homogeneity tests combine L-comoments of several orders and both directions. They therefore require the whole matrix \(\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat{\unknown})\). In current practice, this matrix is approximated by simulation from a fitted parametric model (Chebana and Ouarda, 2007). For these reasons, the main aim of this paper is to derive the exact finite-sample form of \(\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat{\unknown})\) for every fixed _n_, without a parametric model, and to estimate this matrix unbiasedly and efficiently from the data. First-order covariance approximations for the ratios \(\tau_m^{[XY]}\) and \(\tau_m^{[YX]}\) of Section 2 are given in Appendix E.

## 3 Exact finite-sample covariance

In this section we derive the exact finite-sample covariance matrix \(\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat{\unknown})\) for any fixed _n_, without assuming a parametric form for the dependence between _X_ and _Y_ . Theorem 3.1 expresses this matrix through the conditional means of the kernels defined below. Section 3.1 gives these conditional means explicitly, and Section 3.2 obtains the covariance in closed form when _X_ and _Y_ are independent.

## Overlap identity.

Since sample L-comoments are U-statistics, their covariances follow from a standard identity of U-statistic theory. The idea is as follows. Each sample L-comoment is an average of kernel values over subsets of the pairs. Consider one kernel value of \(\widehat{\lambda}_m^a\), computed from a subset _I_ of _m_ pairs, and one kernel value of \(\widehat{\lambda}_s^b\), computed from a subset _J_ of _s_ pairs. If _I_ and _J_ have no pair in common, the two kernel values are independent, because the pairs are independent; hence their covariance is zero. If _I_ and _J_ share \(c\ge 1\) pairs, the two kernel values are dependent only through these _c_ shared pairs. Given the shared pairs, the two kernel values are independent, so their covariance is the covariance of their conditional means given the shared pairs.

We therefore define the conditional mean of a kernel given _c_ of its pairs, which we call a conditional kernel. For \(a\in\{[XY],[YX]\}\) and \(1\le c\le m\), let

\(M_{m,c}^a(z_1,\dots,z_c)=\mathbb{E}(H_m^a(Z_1,\dots,Z_m)|Z_1=z_1,\dots,Z_c=z_c),\) (3.1)

which averages the kernel over the remaining _m-c_ pairs. In particular, \(M_{m,m}^a=H_m^a\). By the law of iterated expectations and \(\mathbb{E}\{H_m^a(Z_1,\dots,Z_m)\}=\lambda_m^a\) (Section 2),<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}\{M_{m,c}^a(Z_1,\dots,Z_c)\}=\lambda_m^a.\)

<tbc>The case _c_=1 plays a special role. The function \(M_{m,1}^a(z)\) is the mean of the kernel when one of its _m_ pairs is fixed at _z_, and it is called the _first projection_ of the kernel \(H_m^a\) (Hoeffding, 1948; Serfling, 1980). The name comes from the fact that

\(\frac{m}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\{M_{m,1}^a(Z_i)-\lambda_m^a\}\) (3.2)

is the projection of \(\widehat{\lambda}_m^a-\lambda_m^a\) onto sums of the form \(\sum_{i=1}^ng(Z_i)\), that is, the sum of functions of single observations that is closest to \(\widehat{\lambda}_m^a-\lambda_m^a\) in mean square. This sum determines the leading term of the covariance of \(\widehat{\lambda}_m^a\) (Section 4). Let each of _a_ and _b_ denote one of the two directions, \[_XY_\] or \[_YX_\], and let each of _m_ and _s_ denote one of the orders, 2 or 3. For \(1\le c\le min(m,s)\), define

\(\Gamma_{ms,c}^{ab}=Cov\{M_{m,c}^a(Z_1,\dots,Z_c),M_{s,c}^b(Z_1,\dots,Z_c)\}=\mathbb{E}(M_{m,c}^aM_{s,c}^b)-\lambda_m^a\lambda_s^b.\) (3.3)

By the argument above, \(\Gamma_{ms,c}^{ab}\) is the covariance between a kernel value of \(\widehat{\lambda}_m^a\) and a kernel value of \(\widehat{\lambda}_s^b\) whose subsets share exactly _c_ pairs. For fixed _m_, _s_, and _c_, we collect the four values of \(\Gamma_{ms,c}^{ab}\) in the \(2\times 2\) matrix

\(\unknown_{ms,c}=\left(\begin{array}{ c c }

\(a_n=\frac{n+1}{3n(n-1)},b_n=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{5n(n-1)(n-2)}.\) (3.13)

_In particular, the estimators_ \(\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[XY]}\) _and_ \(\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[YX]}\) _of the two directions have the positive covariance_ \(\ell_2^X\ell_2^Y/(n-1)\)_, although X and Y are independent._

Under independence, the population L-comoments vanish: by (2.3),

\(\lambda_m^{[XY]}=\mathbb{E}(X)\mathbb{E}[P_{m-1}\{F_Y(Y)\}]=0,m\ge 2,\)

because _F<sub>Y</sub>(Y_) is uniform on (0,1) and \(\int_0^1P_{m-1}(u)du=0\). Their estimators, however, are computed from the same _n_ pairs: \(\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[XY]}\) weights the _X_ values by the ranks of the _Y_ values,<tbc>

and \(\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[YX]}\) weights the _Y_ values by the ranks of the _X_ values. A pair with large values of both _X_ and _Y_ therefore increases both estimators, and a pair with a large _X_ value and a small _Y_ value decreases both. Hence the chance association in the sample moves the two estimators together, and their covariance is positive even though _X_ and _Y_ are independent. For the proof of Theorem 3.4, Appendix B derives each matrix entry from the weighted-sum form (2.8) and the concomitant representation (2.4) (Hosking, 1990; Serfling and Xiao, 2007).

The opposite-direction covariances are not a small-sample artifact. By Theorem 3.4, the correlation of the two second-order estimators is

\(\mathrm{Corr}\big(\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[XY]},\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[YX]}\big)=\frac{\ell_2^X\ell_2^Y/(n-1)}{a_n\{\mathrm{Var}(X)\mathrm{Var}(Y)\}^{1/2}}=\frac{3n}{n+1}\frac{\ell_2^X\ell_2^Y}{\{\mathrm{Var}(X)\mathrm{Var}(Y)\}^{1/2}},\)

which converges to \(3\ell_2^X\ell_2^Y/\{\mathrm{Var}(X)\mathrm{Var}(Y)\}^{1/2}\) rather than to zero; for normal margins, where \(\ell_2=\sigma/\sqrt{\pi}\) with \(\sigma\) the standard deviation of the margin, the limit is \(3/\pi\approx 0.95\). Hence, even when _X_ and _Y_ are independent, the estimators of the two directions carry largely overlapping information, and their covariance matrix has substantial off-diagonal entries.

This has three practical implications. First, joint inference on both directions, for example a test of \(\lambda_2^{[XY]}=\lambda_2^{[YX]}=0\) or of \(\lambda_2^{[XY]}=\lambda_2^{[YX]}\), must use the joint covariance. Since the two estimators are positively correlated, treating them as independent overstates the variance of \(\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[XY]}-\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[YX]}\) and understates that of \(\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[XY]}+\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[YX]}\). Second, covariance-weighted procedures, such as generalized L-moment estimation with inverse covariance weighting (Shin et al., 2026) and minimum-distance fitting of L-comoments, should use the full covariance matrix. A diagonal weight matrix ignores this correlation and leads to inefficient estimators and incorrect standard errors. The full matrix, however, can be nearly singular, which motivates the positive-definite (PD) regularization in Remark 5.4. Third, the estimators of the two directions carry largely the same information. Suppose that both \(\lambda_2^{[XY]}\) and \(\lambda_2^{[YX]}\) are used as moment conditions, for example when a bivariate model is fitted by matching L-comoments. Then the second condition adds little to the first. Under independence with normal margins, for instance, the correlation of the two estimators is close to 0.95. This redundancy should be taken into account when the moment conditions are chosen.

## 4.2 A consistent estimator of the leading covariance

For asymptotic inference, only the leading term \(\Omega/n\) in (4.8) is needed, because the remaining terms are of order _n_<sup>-2</sup>. The leading term has a simple structure: by (4.7), \(\Omega\) is the covariance matrix of the centered and scaled first projections \(\unknown(Z)\). We therefore estimate \(\Omega\) by the sample covariance matrix of estimated first projections. A matrix of this form is PSD for any observed data set, not only on average or in the limit, which is convenient when the estimate must be inverted.

The first projection \(M_{m,1}^a(z)\) (Section 3) is the mean of the kernel \(H_m^a\) when one of its _m_ pairs is fixed at _z_ and the other _m_-1 pairs are drawn from the distribution of (_X,Y_). \(\widehat{M}_{m,1}(Z_i)=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-1}{m-1}^{-1}\sum_{J\subset\{1,\dots,n\}\backslash\{i\}|J|=m-1}\mathbf{H}_m(Z_i,Z_J),i=1,\dots,n.\) (4.10)

## 4.3 An exactly unbiased estimator of the finite-sample covariance

The projection estimator of Theorem 4.4 targets only the leading term \(\Omega/n\). It omits the corrections \(B_2/\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}\) and \(B_3/\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{3}\), which are not negligible for the sample sizes of 20 to 50 that are common in applications; in Section 6.3, the projection estimator understates the variances by up to about 14% at _n_=20. When standard errors should not be understated, an estimator of the exact finite-sample covariance is needed. We now construct an exactly unbiased one. It applies the standard U-statistic disjoint-subset principle (Hoeffding, 1948; Serfling, 1980), which is stated in Appendix A (paragraph "Disjoint-subset principle"). Unlike the projection estimator, it need not be PSD in a given sample; Remark 5.4 below gives PSD and PD corrections. In the univariate L-moment setting, a related exact unbiased construction was given by Elamir and Seheult (2004). The present result concerns the joint sampling covariance of the L-comoments; it is not a new general unbiasedness theorem.

### Disjoint pairs of index sets.

Each sample statistic is an average of kernel values over index sets. In the product of two statistics, a kernel value of the first statistic, computed on an index set _I_, is multiplied by a kernel value of the second statistic, computed on an index set _J_. We call (_I,J_) an ordered pair of index sets: _I_ belongs to the first kernel and _J_ to the second. The pair is _disjoint_ if \(I\cap J=\varnothing\), that is, if the two kernel values share no observation. This is the case _c_=0 in the overlap identity (3.4); the other pairs share \(c=|I\cap J|\ge 1\) observations. Because the pairs _Z_<sub>1</sub>_,...,Z<sub>n</sub>_ are independent, the two kernel values of a disjoint pair are independent, and the expectation of their product is the product of their means. Averaging the products over all disjoint pairs (_I,J_) therefore estimates the product of the means without bias. Subtracting this average from the product of the two statistics gives an unbiased estimator of their covariance.<tbc>

**Theorem 4.8** (Disjoint-subset unbiased covariance construction)**.** _Let_ \(U_{n,m}^a\) _and_ \(U_{n,s}^b\) _be any two of the following complete U-statistics: the sample means (order one, with kernels_ \(H_1^{[XY]}(z)=x\) _and_ \(H_1^{[YX]}(z)=y\)_), the sample L-comoments (_\(a\in\{[XY],[YX]\}\)_), and the marginal sample L-moments (_\(a\in\{[XX],[YY]\}\)_, with the kernels_ \(H_m^{[XX]}\) _and_ \(H_m^{[YY]}\) _of Corollary 4.5) of orders two and three. The kernel orders are_ \(m,s\in\{1,2,3\}\)_. For_ \(n\ge m+s\)_, define_ \(D_{ms,n}^{ab}=\frac{1}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{m}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-m}{s}}\sum_{|I|=m}\sum_{|J|=sI\cap J=\emptyset} H_m^a(Z_I)H_s^b(Z_J).\) (4.12) _Then_ \(\widehat{C}_{ms,n}^{ab}=U_{n,m}^aU_{n,s}^b-D_{ms,n}^{ab},\mathbb{E}(\widehat{C}_{ms,n}^{ab})=\mathrm{Cov}(U_{n,m}^a,U_{n,s}^b).\) (4.13) _In particular, the conditions are_ \(n\ge 2,3,4\) _for the order pairs_ (1,1),(1,2),(1,3)_, respectively, and_ \(n\ge 4,5,6\) _for_ (2,2),(2,3),(3,3)_. Thus the entire enlarged covariance, including the_ \(6\times 6\) _sampling covariance matrix of the sample means and L-comoments, admits an exactly unbiased estimator for_ \(n\ge 6\). _Proof._ The U-statistics \(U_{n,m}^a,U_{n,s}^b\) are unbiased for \(\lambda_m^a,\lambda_s^b\). Every term of \(D_{ms,n}^{ab}\) evaluates the first kernel on _I_ and the second kernel on _J_, where (_I,J_) is a disjoint pair of index sets. Since the pairs are independent, for each term \(\mathbb{E}(H_m^a(Z_I)H_s^b(Z_J))=\mathbb{E}(H_m^a(Z_I))\mathbb{E}(H_s^b(Z_J))=\lambda_m^a\lambda_s^b.\) The denominator in (4.12) is the number \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{m}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-m}{s}\) of such disjoint pairs, hence \(\mathbb{E}(D_{ms,n}^{ab})=\lambda_m^a\lambda_s^b\). Finally \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{C}_{ms,n}^{ab})=\mathbb{E}(U_{n,m}^aU_{n,s}^b)-\lambda_m^a\lambda_s^b\)
\(=\mathrm{Cov}(U_{n,m}^a,U_{n,s}^b).\) Exchanging the roles of _I_ and _J_, together with the two statistics, shows that \(\widehat{C}_{sm,n}^{ba}=\widehat{C}_{ms,n}^{ab}\), so the assembled matrix is symmetric. PSD and positive-definite corrections are given in Section 5.2. **Corollary 4.9** (First-order consistency)**.** _Assume_ \(\mathbb{E}(X^2+Y^2)<\infty\)_, and let_ \(\widehat{C}_n\) _be the full unbiased covariance estimator of_ \(\widehat{T}_n\) _assembled from_ (4.13)_, for_ \(n\ge 6\)_. _Proof._ For orders \(m,s\le 3\), let _V<sub>c,n</sub>_ average \(H_m^a(Z_I)H_s^b(Z_J)\) over pairs of index sets with \(|I\cap J|=c\). With \(p_{c,n}=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{c}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-m}{s-c}/\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{s}\) and \(V_{0,n}=D_{ms,n}^{ab}\), the overlap decomposition gives

\(\widehat{C}_{ms,n}^{ab}=\sum_{c=1}^{min(m,s)}p_{c,n}\{V_{c,n}-V_{0,n}\}.\)

For each fixed _c_, _V<sub>c,n</sub>_ is a symmetrized U-statistic of order _m+s-c_ with an integrable product kernel, by Cauchy-Schwarz. The strong law of large numbers for fixed-order U-statistics (Serfling, 1980) gives \(V_{c,n}\rightarrow v_c\) almost surely. \(n\widehat{C}_{ms,n}^{ab}\longrightarrow^{\mathrm{a}.\mathrm{s}.}ms\mathrm{Cov}\{M_{m,1}^a(Z),M_{s,1}^b(Z)\}.\)

Applied to every entry of the enlarged moment vector, this limit is \(\Omega\). Theorem 4.4 then gives the second assertion in (4.14).

## 5.2 PSD and positive-definite corrections

Unbiasedness holds entry by entry and on average over repeated samples. It does not imply that the matrix computed from the observed sample is PSD: the assembled estimator can have negative eigenvalues, especially for small _n_ ( 3). We therefore consider its PSD correction. Let \(\|A\|_F=\{\mathrm{tr}(A^\mathsf{T}A)\}^{1/2}=(\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2)^{1/2}\) denote the Frobenius norm. The PSD correction \(\widehat{C}_n^+\) of a symmetric matrix \(\widehat{C}_n\) is its Frobenius projection onto the set of PSD matrices (Higham, 1988), that is, the PSD matrix _A_ that minimizes \(\|A-\widehat{C}_n\|_F\). If \(\widehat{C}_n=V\mathrm{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_p)V^\mathsf{T}\) is the spectral decomposition, where _p_ is the dimension of the moment vector, then \(\widehat{C}_n^+=V\mathrm{diag}\{\mathrm{max}(d_1,0),\dots,\mathrm{max}(d_p,0)\}V^\mathsf{T}\); that is, the negative eigenvalues are replaced by zero.

**Corollary 5.3** (PSD correction)**.** _Under the conditions of Corollary 4.9,_ \(\widehat{C}_n^+\unknown 0\) _for any observed data set and_

\(n\widehat{C}_n^+\longrightarrow^{\mathrm{a}.\mathrm{s}.}\Omega.\) (5.7)

_Proof._ Projection onto the closed convex set of PSD matrices is continuous and commutes with multiplication by a nonnegative scalar, so \(n\widehat{C}_n^+=(n\widehat{C}_n)^+\). Since \(n\widehat{C}_n\rightarrow\Omega\) almost surely by Corollary 4.9 and \(\Omega\unknown 0\), we obtain \((n\widehat{C}_n)^+\rightarrow\Omega^+=\Omega\) almost surely.

The PSD correction thus retains first-order consistency, but it generally does not preserve exact unbiasedness. Indeed, \(\widehat{C}_n^+-\widehat{C}_n\) is PSD and is nonzero whenever \(\widehat{C}_n\) has a negative<tbc>

eigenvalue. Hence \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{C}_n^+)-\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat{T}_n)\) is PSD, and it is nonzero whenever \(\widehat{C}_n\) is indefinite with positive probability. When the estimate must be inverted, a positive-definite (PD) correction is needed as well.

_Remark_ 5.4 (PSD and positive-definite correction). Write _C<sub>n</sub>_ for the true finite-sample covariance matrix of the moment vector, for example \(C_n=\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat{T}_n)\). The eigenvalue truncation below is the nearest symmetric PSD matrix in Frobenius norm (Higham, 1988); related eigenvalue- constrained covariance estimation is discussed by Liu et al. (2014). Write \(\mathcal{S}_n=n\widehat{C}_n=V_n\mathrm{diag}(d_{1n},\dots,d_{pn})V_n^\mathsf{T}\). Its PSD correction replaces _d<sub>jn</sub>_ by \(d_{jn}^+=\mathrm{max}(d_{jn},0)\); since _C<sub>n</sub>_ is PSD, projection also gives \(\|\widehat{C}_n^+-C_n\|_F\le\|\widehat{C}_n-C_n\|_F\). For inversion, choose \(\varepsilon_n>0\) with \(\varepsilon_n\rightarrow 0\) and define

\(\widehat{C}_n^\mathrm{PD}=\frac{1}{n}V_n\mathrm{diag}\{\mathrm{max}(d_{1n},\varepsilon_n),\dots,\mathrm{max}(d_{pn},\varepsilon_n)\}V_n^\mathsf{T}.\) (5.8)

Then \(\widehat{C}_n^\mathrm{PD}\succ 0\) for any observed data set and \(n\widehat{C}_n^\mathrm{PD}\rightarrow\Omega\) almost surely. If \(\Omega\succ 0\), the inverse of the corrected _scaled_ covariance converges to \(\Omega^{-1}\). When \(\Omega\) is singular, PD regularization does not make a consistent estimator of a nonexistent \(\Omega^{-1}\). Neither PSD nor PD correction generally retains finite-sample unbiasedness.

The statistical properties of the two corrections can be summarized as follows.

(a) _Consistency._ Both corrections preserve first-order consistency: \(n\widehat{C}_n^+\rightarrow\Omega\) by Corollary 5.3, and \(\|n\widehat{C}_n^\mathrm{PD}-n\widehat{C}_n^+\|_F\le p^{1/2}\varepsilon_n\rightarrow 0\) because the two matrices differ only in eigenvalues below \(\varepsilon_n\).<tbc>

(b) _Unbiasedness._ Neither correction is unbiased. Since \(\widehat{C}_n^\mathrm{PD}\unknown\widehat{C}_n^+\unknown\widehat{C}_n\) in the Loewner order, both corrections shift the estimator upward, and the shift is nonzero on the event that \(\widehat{C}_n\) is indefinite.  3 shows that this bias is small for the PSD projection.<tbc>

(c) _Singular limit._ If \(\Omega\) is singular, for example when some linear combination of the moments has a degenerate first-order projection, the corrected matrices remain consistent for \(\Omega\). Their smallest eigenvalues, however, tend to zero, and inverse-covariance weighting is ill-posed in the limit. A generalized inverse or a reduced moment vector is then more appropriate than inversion of \(\widehat{C}_n^\mathrm{PD}\).<tbc>

(d) _Role of_ \(\varepsilon_n\). The floor \(\varepsilon_n\) guarantees invertibility for any observed data set and bounds the condition number of \(n\widehat{C}_n^\mathrm{PD}\) by \(\mathrm{max}_jd_{jn}/\varepsilon_n\); the condition \(\varepsilon_n\rightarrow 0\) ensures that the regularization vanishes asymptotically. A larger floor stabilizes the inverse at the cost of more upward bias. Our implementation uses \(\varepsilon_n=n^{-1}p^{-1}\sum_j|d_{jn}|\), which is _O(n_<sup>-1</sup>); in the Gaussian design of Section 6.3, its median is 0.020 and 0.008 for _n_=20 and 50, about 1% of the largest eigenvalue of \(n\widehat{C}_n\).<tbc>

## 7 Discussion

The results of this study are potentially relevant to multivariate regional frequency analysis (Chebana and Ouarda, 2007; Akinsoji et al., 2026). In the discordancy and homogeneity tests of Chebana and Ouarda (2007), the dispersion of at-site L-comoment coefficients is weighted by record length, and its null distribution is obtained by simulating homogeneous regions from a fitted bivariate model, whose choice the authors note is subjective. The present estimators give the sampling covariance of each site’s L-comoments from the site’s own data, without a parametric model. They could potentially provide precision weights in place of weights based on record length, and they may serve as a basis for a simulation-free approximation to the null distribution of such statistics. These tests also use fourth-order L-comoment coefficients; the projection estimator covers them (Corollary 4.6), whereas the exactly unbiased estimator of order four requires the algorithmic extension noted in Remark 4.7. These order-four results follow directly from fixed-order U-statistic theory and the leave-one-out identity, and we include them as a supplementary extension because of this use in practice. Spatial dependence between sites, studied by Šimková (2017), is outside our assumption of independent pairs.

When _X_ and _Y_ are measured on the same scale, the symmetric component \(S_m=(\lambda_m^{[XY]}+\lambda_m^{[YX]})/2\) and the difference between the two directions \(D_m=(\lambda_m^{[XY]}-\lambda_m^{[YX]})/2\) may also be of interest; symmetric Gini constructions are studied by Sang et al. (2016). Following Serfling and Xiao (2007), we treated the ordered pair \((\lambda_m^{[XY]},\lambda_m^{[YX]})\) as the basic object. The vector \((\widehat{S}_2,\widehat{D}_2,\widehat{S}_3,\widehat{D}_3)^\mathsf{T}\) equals \(\mathsf{A}\widehat{\unknown}\), where A is block diagonal with two blocks \(\frac{1}{2}\big(\frac{1}{1}\frac{1}{1}\big)\). Its exact covariance is therefore \(\mathsf{A}\mathsf{Cov}(\widehat{\unknown})\mathsf{A}^\mathsf{T}\) by Theorem 3.1; as noted in Section 3.2, ignoring the correlation between the two directions overstates the variance of \(\widehat{D}_m\). Under exchangeability, (_X,Y_)=<sup>_d_</sup>(_Y,X_), we have \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{D}_m)=0\) and \(\mathsf{Cov}(\widehat{S}_m,\widehat{D}_s)=0\) for \(m,s\in\{2,3\}\), which could serve as the basis of a test of exchangeability. Related tests based on the difference between the two directional Gini coefficients, such as the test for time reversibility of Shelef and Schechtman (2019), have relied on bootstrap approximations; for independent pairs, the exact covariance offers an alternative.

For routine asymptotic standard errors, the projection-based PSD estimator is a natural default. When finite-sample bias should be avoided, the unbiased estimator or its PSD projection is preferable, whereas the projection-based estimator can be preferable under squared-error loss for the whole covariance matrix (Section 6.3). For the ratio \(\widehat{\tau}_3\), the first-order approximation can overstate the variance under heavy-tailed margins, by up to 29% at _n_=20 in our GEV design (Appendix E.1). The exact covariance results extend those of Elamir and Seheult (2004) for univariate L-moments to L-comoments, and the rank-prefix algorithm of Section 5 makes the corresponding unbiased estimator practical for large samples. PSD and PD regularizations based on eigenvalue correction (Higham, 1988; Liu et al., 2014) are available when a covariance- matrix form or an inverse is required, although they generally sacrifice exact unbiasedness.<tbc>

<tbc>Downstream inference based on multivariate L-moment estimation also requires identification and appropriate moment Jacobians. Inverse covariance weighting (Shin et al., 2026) further requires a nonsingular limiting covariance.

The results assume independent observation pairs and continuous margins, with unrestricted dependence within each pair. Higher-order L-comoments, L-comoment matrices of more than two variables, and trimmed L-comoments (Elamir and Seheult, 2003; Hosking, 2007) are again fixed-order U-statistics. The overlap formula, exact unbiasedness, and consistency therefore extend directly; only the conditional kernels and the rank-prefix tables must be redeveloped. Ties can be handled with a kernel convention, such as sgn(0)=0 and averaging over tied orderings. This convention keeps the above properties but changes the targets, the closed forms, and the algorithm. For the _r_ largest observations of blocks (Tawn, 1988; Busabodhin et al., 2025, 2026), the present results apply when the blocks are independent, because the dependence among the order statistics within a block is allowed.

## 8 Conclusion

We derived the exact finite-sample covariance structure of sample L-comoments in both directions, for bivariate samples with unrestricted dependence within each pair. Explicit conditional kernels give every entry of the exact \(4\times 4\) sampling covariance matrix and its \(6\times 6\) extension that includes the sample means. They also yield a canonical Hoeffding decomposition of this covariance. When _X_ and _Y_ are independent, the covariance matrix is fully explicit and shows that the estimators of the two directions are correlated even when both population L-comoments vanish. We considered two estimators of this sampling covariance matrix. The first is exactly unbiased for the finite-sample covariance, is first-order consistent, and can be corrected to be PSD or PD. The second is a projection estimator of the leading asymptotic covariance, which is consistent and PSD for any observed data set.

An overlap inclusion-exclusion identity combined with rank-prefix sums evaluates the unbiased estimator in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time instead of _O(n_<sup>6</sup>). The numerical experiments confirmed the exact formulas and the agreement of the fast and direct algorithms. For samples of size 20-50, the unbiased estimator had no detectable bias, whereas the projection estimator understated the covariance by several percent. The projection estimator nevertheless had the smaller root mean squared error, so the choice between the two estimators is a bias-variance trade-off. The first-order approximation for L-comoment ratios was accurate except for \(\widehat{\tau}_3\) under heavy-tailed margins, where it overstated the variance. These results may be useful in subsequent studies of inference based on L-comoments, for example in tests of independence or exchangeability, in the discordancy and homogeneity tests of regional frequency analysis, and in multivariate L-moment estimation with inverse-covariance weighting.

## Overlap formula.

Let _U<sub>n</sub>_ and _V<sub>n</sub>_ be U-statistics with kernels _h_ of order _m_ and _g_ of order _s_. Then

\(\text{Cov}(U_n,V_n)=\sum_{c=1}^{min(m,s)}\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{c}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-m}{s-c}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{s}}\text{Cov}\{h_c(Z_1,\dots,Z_c),g_c(Z_1,\dots,Z_c)\}.\) (A.1)

Terms with disjoint index sets contribute zero, and a term whose index sets share _c_ observations contributes the covariance of the conditional kernels given those observations (Hoeffding, 1948).

## Hoeffding decomposition.

Define the canonical kernels recursively by \(h^{(1)}(z_1)=h_1(z_1)-\theta\) and, for \(c\ge 2\),<tbc>

\(h^{(c)}(z_1,\dots,z_c)=h_c(z_1,\dots,z_c)-\theta-\sum_{j=1}^{c-1}\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_j\le c}h^{(j)}(z_{i_1},\dots,z_{i_j}).\)

<tbc>Each _h_<sup>(_c_)</sup> has zero conditional mean given any proper subset of its arguments. With \(U_n^{(c)}=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{c}^{-1}\sum_{|I|=c}h^{(c)}(Z_I)\),

\(U_n-\theta=\sum_{c=1}^m\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{c}U_n^{(c)},\) (A.2)

and the terms are uncorrelated across _c_. In particular, \(\text{Var}(U_n)=\sum_{c=1}^m\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{c}^2\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{c}^{-1}\text{Var}\{h^{(c)}\}\), whose leading term is _m_<sup>2</sup>Var{_h_<sub>1</sub>(_Z_<sub>1</sub>)}_/n_ (Lee, 1990).

### Limit theorems. By the strong law of large numbers for U-statistics, \(U_n\rightarrow\theta\) almost surely when \(\mathbb{E}|h|<\infty\) (Serfling, 1980, Chapter 5). By the central limit theorem, \(\sqrt{n}(U_n-\theta)\rightarrow^dN(0,m^2\mathrm{Var}\{h_1(Z_1)\})\); the multivariate version holds jointly for finitely many U-statistics, with asymptotic covariance _ms_Cov{_h_1(_Z_1)_,g_1(_Z_1)} between kernels of orders _m_ and _s_ (Serfling, 1980, Chapter 5). These results, combined with the delta method (van der Vaart, 1998), give the limits of smooth functions such as ratios. ### Leave-one-out identity. Let \(\widehat{h}_1(Z_i)=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-1}{m-1}^{-1}\sum_{I\unknown i,|I|=m}h(Z_I)\) be the average of the kernel over the subsets containing observation _i_, and let \(U_{n-1}^{(-i)}\) be the U-statistic computed from the sample without observation _i_. If _I_ and _J_ are disjoint, _h(ZI_) and _g(ZJ_) are independent, so E{_h(ZI)g(ZJ_)}=E(_h_)E(_g_). Averaging such products over all disjoint pairs (_I,J_) therefore gives an unbiased estimator of the product of means, and subtracting it from _UnVn_ gives an unbiased estimator of Cov(_Un,Vn_) (Hoeffding, 1948). ### Inclusion-exclusion. For finite index sets _I_ and _J_, \(\mathbf{1}\{I\cap J=\varnothing\}=\sum_{K\subseteq I\cap J}(-1)^{|K|}\). ## C Rank-prefix computation of the exact unbiased covariance

Here we justify the complexity assertion of Proposition 5.1. The combinatorial argument uses fixed-order U-statistic incidence counting (Serfling, 1980); the range-sum implementation uses two-dimensional prefix tables (Crow, 1984). Write the _p_ kernels in one vector, with orders \(m_a\in\{1,2,3\}\). For \(|K|=c\le m_a\) define the uncentered incidence sums

\(\mathcal{I}_{a,K}=\sum_{I\supseteq K|I|=m_a}H_{m_a}^a(Z_I),N_a=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{m_a},U_a=\mathcal{I}_{a,\emptyset}/N_a.\) (C.1)

Then \(A_{m_a,K}^a=\mathcal{I}_{a,K}-\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-c}{m_a-c}U_a\). Consequently, only singleton, pair, and triple incidence products are required in (5.2). The order-one and order-two incidence sums are immediate after _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) pairwise evaluations.

For the order-three kernels, fix a pair _i\<j_, and denote its ordered _Y_ -ranks by \(\ell_Y<h_Y\). The third observation _k_ belongs to one of the three open _Y_ -rank intervals \([1,\ell_Y-1]\), \([\ell_Y+1,h_Y-1]\), or \[_h<sub>Y</sub>_+1_,n_\]. Within each interval the forward kernel is an affine function

\(H_3^{[XY]}(Z_i,Z_j,Z_k)=(aX_k+b)/3,a\in\{1,-2,1\},\)

where _b_ depends only on the fixed pair and on its rank interval. One-dimensional cumulative counts and sums of _X_ in increasing _Y_ -rank order therefore evaluate the forward component of _F<sub>ij</sub>_ in constant time for each pair.

The reverse component follows analogously from cumulative counts and sums of _Y_ in _X_-rank order. The endpoints are _excluded_: neither _k=i_ nor _k=j_ has a rank in any of the three open intervals for the relevant ranking coordinate. Thus no separate endpoint subtraction is required.

For cross-direction products, partition the third observation by both its _X_- and _Y_ -rank intervals, giving nine open rank rectangles. In each rectangle the two kernels have the forms (_aX<sub>k</sub>+b)/_3 and (_cY<sub>k</sub>+d)/_3. Their product is<tbc>

\(\frac{acX_kY_k+adX_k+bcY_k+bd}{9},\)

which is linear in each variable and of total degree at most two, not quadratic in each variable. Squaring a kernel of a single direction instead produces \(X_k^2\) or \(Y_k^2\).

Construct two-dimensional prefix tables on the joint rank grid for<tbc>

\(1,X,Y,X^2,Y^2,XY.\) (C.2)

<tbc>Each open rectangle contributes its count, first moments, and quadratic moments through four prefix-table lookups. The rectangle boundaries use the ranks of _i_ and _j_, so both anchor observations are omitted from all nine rectangles. Empty intervals and rectangles contribute zero. Consequently, for each fixed pair, the vector and matrix

\(F_{ij}=\sum_{k\neq i,j}\mathbf{H}_3(Z_i,Z_j,Z_k),G_{ij}=\sum_{k\neq i,j}\mathbf{H}_3(Z_i,Z_j,Z_k)\mathbf{H}_3(Z_i,Z_j,Z_k)^\top\) (C.3)

Only one-dimensional prefix sums are needed for _F<sub>ij</sub>_; the joint rank rectangles are needed for the off-diagonal, cross-direction entries of _G<sub>ij</sub>_. Its same-direction diagonal entries can also be calculated from one-dimensional prefix sums of squared coordinates.

The resulting singleton and total third-order incidence sums are

\(\sum_{I\unknown i,|I|=3}\mathbf{H}_3(Z_I)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j\neq i}F_{ij},\sum_{|I|=3}\mathbf{H}_3(Z_I)=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{i<j}F_{ij},\sum_{|I|=3}\mathbf{H}_3(Z_I)\mathbf{H}_3(Z_I)^\top=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{i<j}G_{ij}.\) (C.4)

The centered incidence products are formed by subtracting the appropriate multiples of _U<sub>a</sub>_. Thus each of the three overlap levels, and every entry of the fixed-dimensional covariance matrix, is obtained with _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) work after constructing _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) prefix storage. For any vectors **_u_**_,**v**_, \(\|\mathbf{uu}^\mathsf{T}-\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^\mathsf{T}\|_F\le\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\|^2+2\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\). Averaging over _i_ and applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

\(\|\widehat{\Omega}_n-\widetilde{\Omega}_n\|_F\le\Delta_n+2\Delta_n^{1/2}\big(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\|\unknown_i\|^2\big)^{1/2}.\)

By Steps 2 and 3 the right-hand side tends to zero in probability, and hence \(\widehat{\Omega}_n\rightarrow^p\Omega\).

## E First-order covariance of L-comoment ratios

We consider the sample versions of the standardized coefficients \(\tau_m^{[XY]}\) and \(\tau_m^{[YX]}\) of Section 2,

\(\widehat{\tau}_m^{[XY]}=\frac{\widehat{\lambda}_m^{[XY]}}{\widehat{\lambda}_2(X)},\widehat{\tau}_m^{[YX]}=\frac{\widehat{\lambda}_m^{[YX]}}{\widehat{\lambda}_2(Y)},m=2,3.\) (E.1)

The denominators are the marginal sample L-scales of the measured variables. The covariance of these nonlinear ratios is not obtained exactly by linear transformation of the underlying moment covariance. Following Elamir and Seheult (2004), who distinguished exact covariances of sample L-moments from Taylor-approximated standard errors of their ratios, we use the delta method (Oehlert, 1992; van der Vaart, 1998).

**Corollary E.1** (Joint first-order ratio covariance)**.** _Assume the margins are continuous and nondegenerate and_ \(\mathbb{E}(X^2+Y^2)<\infty\)_. Let_<tbc>

\(\widehat{\mathbf{m}}_n=\left(\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[XY]},\widehat{\lambda}_2^{[YX]},\widehat{\lambda}_3^{[XY]},\widehat{\lambda}_3^{[YX]},\widehat{\lambda}_2(X),\widehat{\lambda}_2(Y)\right)^\mathsf{T}\)

<tbc>_be the vector of the four sample L-comoments and the two marginal sample L-scales, and let_ \(\mathbf{m}=\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\mathbf{m}}_n)=(m_1,\dots,m_6)^\mathsf{T}\)_. Denote their exact finite-sample covariance by C<sub>M,n</sub>, and its leading Hoeffding term by_ \(\Omega_M\)_, so that_ \(C_{M,n}=\Omega_M/n+O(n^{-2})\)_. Define the map_ \(g:\mathbb{R}^4\times(0,\infty)^2\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^4\) _by_<tbc>

\(g(m_1,\dots,m_6)=\left(\frac{m_1}{m_5},\frac{m_2}{m_6},\frac{m_3}{m_5},\frac{m_4}{m_6}\right)^\mathsf{T},\)

<tbc>_so that_ \(g(\widehat{\mathbf{m}}_n)=(\widehat{\tau}_2^{[XY]},\widehat{\tau}_2^{[YX]},\widehat{\tau}_3^{[XY]},\widehat{\tau}_3^{[YX]})^\mathsf{T}\) _by_ (E.1)_. Its Jacobian at **m** is_<tbc>

\(J=Dg(\mathbf{m})=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c }
1/m_5 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -m_1/m_5^2 & 0 \\
0 & 1/m_6 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -m_2/m_6^2 \\
0 & 0 & 1/m_5 & 0 & -m_3/m_5^2 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1/m_6 & 0 & -m_4/m_6^2
\end{array}\right).\)

<tbc>_Then_<tbc>

\(\sqrt{n}\{g(\widehat{\mathbf{m}}_n)-g(\mathbf{m})\}\rightarrow^dN_4(0,J\Omega_MJ^\mathsf{T}).\) (E.2)

<tbc>_In particular, if_ \(\widehat{J}_n=Dg(\widehat{\mathbf{m}}_n)\) _and_ \(\widehat{\Omega}_{M,n}\) _is the projection-based covariance estimator for this enlarged moment vector, then_<tbc>

\(\widehat{V}_{\tau,n}=n^{-1}\widehat{J}_n\widehat{\Omega}_{M,n}\widehat{J}_n^\mathsf{T},n\widehat{V}_{\tau,n}\rightarrow^pJ\Omega_MJ^\mathsf{T}.\) (E.3)

<tbc>_For arbitrary ratios R=A/B and S=C/D, write r_=E(_A)/_E(_B), s_=E(_C)/_E(_D), b_=E(_B)\>_0_, and d_=E(_D)\>_0_. A first-order Taylor approximation to their covariance, when defined, is_<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Cov}(R,S)\approx\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(A,C)-s\mathrm{Cov}(A,D)-r\mathrm{Cov}(B,C)+rs\mathrm{Cov}(B,D)}{bd},\) (E.4)

<tbc>_where the terms on the right are entries of C<sub>M,n</sub> and hence admit exact finite-sample covariance formulas. Equation_ (E.4) _is_ not _an exact covariance identity for the ratios._

_Proof._ The appended marginal L-moments are fixed-order U-statistics, so the multivariate Hoeffding central limit theorem applies (Hoeffding, 1948; Serfling, 1980). Their population L-scales are positive; applying the delta method to _g_ proves (E.2). The estimator \(\widehat{\Omega}_{M,n}\) is consistent by Corollary 4.5, and \(\widehat{J}_n\rightarrow_pJ\); continuous mapping yields (E.3). The derivative of _a/b_ is _b_<sup>-1</sup>(d_a-r_d_b_), and expanding the covariance of the resulting linear combinations gives (E.4).

_Remark_ E.2 (Scope of the ratio approximation). The ratio estimators are generally not exactly unbiased, even though their numerator and denominator moment estimators are. Likewise, inserting an exactly unbiased estimate of _C<sub>M,n</sub>_ into the linearized covariance formula does not give an exactly unbiased estimate of the covariance of the nonlinear ratios. First-order linearization is sufficient for the limiting covariance in (E.2). Higher-order corrections involve the third and fourth moments of the moment estimators and additional remainder control, and are not pursued here. Appendix E.1 shows that the linearization can overstate the variance of \(\widehat{\tau}_3\) noticeably under heavy-tailed margins.

### E.1 Accuracy of first-order ratio approximations

With the notation of Section 6 and the three designs of Section 6.3, we also examined the first-order ratio approximation of Corollary E.1. For each ratio \(\widehat{\tau}\) in (E.1), we computed two variances. The Taylor variance is the corresponding diagonal entry of _JC<sub>n</sub>J_<sup>T</sup>, the first-order approximation of Corollary E.1 evaluated with the reference covariance _C<sub>n</sub>_ and the Jacobian _J_ at the population moments. The Monte Carlo variance is the sample variance of \(\widehat{\tau}\) over the 10<sup>6</sup> reference replications, which serves as the true finite-sample variance.  5 reports the ratio of the Taylor variance to the Monte Carlo variance, averaged over the two directions, which gave nearly identical values; a value above one means that the Taylor approximation overstates the variance.

The Taylor variance is within 8% of the Monte Carlo variance for \(\tau_2\) in all designs and for \(\tau_3\) in the independent and Gaussian designs, and the discrepancy decreases with _n_. For \(\tau_3\) under heavy-tailed GEV margins, however, it overstates the variance by 29%, 23%, and 16% at _n_=20, 30, and 50. This agrees with Remark E.2: for small samples and heavy tails, higher-order corrections may be needed for ratio inference.
